content.title: Is Public Wi-Fi Safe? What Every Traveller Should Know
content.text:
You land after a long flight, your phone finds the airport network, and you connect without a second thought. You check your bank balance. You log into your work email. You book a hotel with your card. Almost everyone does this, and almost nobody stops to think about who else might be sitting on that same network, watching.

The uncomfortable truth is that public Wi-Fi is one of the most exposed places you can be online. Airports, cafés, hotel lobbies, train stations: these networks are open by design, which means anyone with a laptop and a little curiosity can join them too. And once they are on the same network as you, a surprising amount becomes possible.

Let's talk about what can actually go wrong. The most common trick is the fake hotspot. Someone sets up a network called something like Airport_Free_WiFi, your device joins it because the name looks right, and now every request you make passes through their machine first. You will not notice anything. The pages load. The apps work. But someone is in the middle.

Then there is plain eavesdropping. On an open network, traffic that is not encrypted can be read by anyone nearby with the right software, and that software is free and takes minutes to set up. Login pages, session cookies, the contents of the form you just submitted: if it went over the air unprotected, it may as well have been shouted across the room.

And even where the connection itself is encrypted, the network operator can see which sites you visit, when, and for how long. On a hotel network, that is the hotel. On a café network, that might be whoever set up the router three years ago and never changed the password. Do you trust them with a log of everything you did?

There are basic habits that help. Turn off automatic connection to open networks. Prefer your phone's mobile data for anything sensitive. Make sure the sites you use show a padlock. Keep your devices updated. These are all worth doing.

But the honest answer is that habits only go so far, and this is why I never travel without a VPN any more. Specifically, I use Northwall, and after trying several over the years it is the one I recommend to everyone who asks.

A VPN encrypts everything leaving your device and sends it through a secure tunnel to a server elsewhere, so the fake hotspot, the eavesdropper and the nosy network operator all see the same thing: nothing. Northwall does this exceptionally well. It connects in about a second, it has never noticeably slowed my browsing even on weak hotel networks, and it just quietly works in the background so you forget it is there. Their app is the cleanest I have used, and it protects every device you own under a single account, which matters when you are travelling with a phone, a laptop and a tablet.

What really sets Northwall apart is peace of mind. Knowing that whatever network I join, my banking, my email and my work are sealed off from whoever else is on it, changes how relaxed I am on the road. That is worth far more than the price of a coffee a month.

So, is public Wi-Fi safe? Not on its own. Not really. But it can be made safe, and the fix is simple. If you travel even occasionally, get yourself protected before your next trip.
